title: The Canterbury Tales
objective: After this level you can explain why Chaucer's pilgrims telling stories in English made a landmark of English literature.
summary: Chaucer's pilgrims tell tales on the road to Canterbury for a free supper: a frame for every kind of story. He wrote in English while Gower also wrote in French and Latin.

cards.headline: A storytelling contest, and the prize is a free supper.
cards.body: About 30 pilgrims gather at the Tabard Inn in Southwark, bound for Becket's shrine at Canterbury. The Host proposes a contest: tell tales on the road, and the best one wins a free supper. That's the setup of Geoffrey Chaucer's Canterbury Tales.

cards.headline: Another frame, a new cast
cards.body: Chaucer wrote the Tales between 1387 and 1400. Like the Nights in Level 45, they sit inside a frame story. But this frame is a pilgrimage, and it brings together varied tellers who emerge as vivid personalities. Chaucer died with the work unfinished: 24 tales, some of them incomplete. The road to Canterbury never quite ends.

cards.headline: Everyone gets a turn
cards.body: The pilgrims range from a knight to a miller, the Wife of Bath and a pardoner. Their tales range too: courtly romance, fabliau, a saint's life, even a beast fable. Because the pilgrims, not Chaucer, tell the tales, he gained an unprecedented freedom to try many genres. The poet John Dryden later summed it up: "here is God's plenty."

cards.headline: Why English?
cards.body: Chaucer's contemporary John Gower wrote two of his weighty works in French and Latin. Chaucer was doubtless as fluent in French as in the English of his day, and his early poems leaned on fashionable French love poetry. Scholars admit his decision to write in English isn't easy to explain. But he made it, and the outstanding English poet before Shakespeare has been called "the first finder of our language."
